Only want to learn from this subset

```{r}
train <- read_csv('data/train.csv')
```

```{r}
train |> 
  filter(total_losses > 0) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=total_losses)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Total Losses (Claimants Only)",
    x     = "Total Losses ($)",
    y     = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The total losses are heavily right skewed and has potential outliers

```{r}
train |> 
  filter(total_losses > 0) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=log(total_losses))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Log Total Losses (Claimants Only)",
    x     = "Log Total Losses",
    y     = "Count",
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The log transformation adjusts the right skewness and contextually, we want to ensure
positive values only, which it also takes care of.

```{r}
bp_stats <- boxplot.stats(train$total_losses[train$total_losses > 0])$stats

upper_fence <- bp_stats[5]
data.frame(
  Stat = c("Lower Fence","Q1", "Median","Q3","Upper fence"),
  Value = bp_stats
)
```
```{r}
train |>
  filter(total_losses > upper_fence) |>
  summarize(
    n_outliers = n(),
    pct_outliers = glue("{round(n()/nrow(train) * 100,2)}%"),
    min_outlier_amount = min(total_losses),
    max_outlier_amount = max(total_losses)
  )

```

```{r}
train |>
  filter(total_losses > upper_fence)
```

This looks fairly random. What's the percentile that our upper fence corresponds to?

```{r}
data.frame(
  CapValue = upper_fence,
  Percentile = glue("{round(mean(train$total_losses[train$total_losses >0] <= upper_fence) * 100,2)}%")
)
```

This is a reasonable percentile, capping with this will not lead us to lose our data so much.
Cap total_losses at the upper fence to reduce the influence of extreme values.

```{r}
train <- train |> 
  mutate(total_losses = pmin(total_losses, upper_fence))

max(train$total_losses)
```

```{r}
summary(train$pure_premium[train$total_losses > 0])
```

# 6. Frequency & Severity Decomposition

Decompose pure premium into frequency (claims per unit exposure)
and severity (average loss per claim), to inform modelling decisions.

```{r}
train <- train |> 
  mutate(frequency = n_claims/policy.Exposure)

summary(train$frequency)
```

Plot of frequency distribution for claim frequency for claimant policies

```{r}
train |> 
  filter(frequency > 0) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = frequency)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "cyan4", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Plot of Claim Frequncy (Claimants only)",
    x = "Claim Frequency",
    y = "Count"
  ) + theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
train <- train |> 
  mutate(severity = ifelse(n_claims > 0, total_losses / n_claims, NA))
summary(train$severity)
```

```{r}
train |> 
  filter(!is.na(severity)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = severity)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "coral3", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Plot of Claim Severity (Claimants only)",
    x = "Claim Severity",
    y = "Count"
  ) + theme_minimal()
```

We see a right skewness.


# 7. Relationship between frequency and severity


```{r}
train |> 
  filter(n_claims > 0) |> 
  summarize(
    correlation = round(cor(frequency, severity), 4)
  )
```

There is no significant correlation between frequency and severity, indicating that
it's not a case of adverse selection.

# 8 Univariate Analysis of Continuous variables

```{r}
univar_analysis_continuous <- function(col, bands = seq(10, 100, by = 10), include.lowest = TRUE) {
  col_name <- rlang::as_name(ensym(col))

  print(train |>
    ggplot(aes(x = {{col}})) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
    labs(
      title = glue("Plot of {col_name}"),
      x = col_name,
      y = "Count"
    )+theme_minimal())

  pp_by_col_band <- train |>
    mutate(!!sym(glue("{col_name}_band")) := cut({{col}},breaks = bands, include.lowest = include.lowest)) |>
    group_by(!!sym(glue("{col_name}_band"))) |>
    summarize(
      n_policies = n(),
      mean_pp = round(mean(pure_premium), 2),
      median_pp = round(median(pure_premium), 2)
    ) |>
    arrange(!!sym(glue("{col_name}_band")))

  print(pp_by_col_band |>
    ggplot(aes(x = !!sym(glue("{col_name}_band")), y = mean_pp)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
    labs(
      title = glue("Mean PP by {col_name} Bands"),
      x = glue("{col_name} Band"),
      y = "Mean PP"
    )+theme_minimal())

  return(pp_by_col_band)
}

univar_analysis_categorical <- function(df, col, head=FALSE){
  col_name <- rlang::as_name(ensym(col))
  print(df |>
    ggplot(aes(x = {{col}})) +
    geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
    labs(
      title = glue("Plot of {col_name}"),
      x = col_name,
      y = "Count"
    )+theme_minimal())
  
  pp_by_col <- df |>
    group_by({{col}}) |>
    summarize(
      n_policies = n(),
      mean_pp = round(mean(pure_premium), 2),
      median_pp = round(median(pure_premium), 2)
    )# |>
    #arrange({{col}})

  print(pp_by_col |>
      ggplot(aes(x = reorder({{col}},mean_pp), y=mean_pp)) +
      geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
      geom_text(aes(label=comma(round(mean_pp,0))), hjust = -0.1, size=3) +
      scale_y_continuous(labels = comma, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
      coord_flip() +
      labs(
        title = glue("Mean PP by {col_name}"),
        x = glue("{col_name}"),
        y = "Mean PP"
      )+theme_minimal()
  )
  
  return(pp_by_col)

}

```

corrplot(cor_matrix,

## 9.2 Relationships between categorical predictors

### pet.Type and pet.Group

Group is a more granular version of Type. We'll check whether Group
already captures the signal from pet.Type

```{r}
train |> 
  group_by(pet.Type) |> 
  summarize(
    n_groups = n_distinct(pet.Group),
    mean_pp = round(mean(pure_premium), 2)
  )
  
```

```{r}
train |>
  group_by(pet.Group, Species = pet.Type) |>
  summarize(
    n_breeds = n_distinct(pet.Breed),
    mean_pp  = round(mean(pure_premium), 2),
    # exp_weighted_pp = round(sum(total_losses)/sum(policy.Exposure),2),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(Species, mean_pp)
  
```

Yes, the pet.Group inherently captures the signal that dogs have twice the pure premium of cats, but further reveals
within-species differentiation (Working dogs average \$456.31 in pp compared to only \$201.42 for Toy dogs).

### pet.Group and pet.Breed

Breed is a more granular version of Group. We'll check whether Breed
already captures the signal from pet.Group


```{r}
train |> 
  group_by(pet.Group) |> 
  summarize(
    n_breeds = n_distinct(pet.Breed),
    mean_pp = round(mean(pure_premium), 2)
  )
```

Let's check which breeds within each group diverge from the group behavior in terms of pure premium.

```{r}
train |>
  group_by(pet.Group) |>
  mutate(group_pp = mean(pure_premium)) |>
  group_by(pet.Group, pet.Breed) |>
  summarize(
    n_policies = n(),
    breed_pp   = mean(pure_premium),
    group_pp   = first(group_pp),
    diff       = breed_pp - group_pp,
    pct_diff   = (breed_pp - group_pp) / group_pp,
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(abs(pct_diff) > 0.70 & n_policies >= 150) |> # >70% divergence
  arrange(desc(abs(pct_diff)))
```

```{r}
breed_outliers <- train |>
  group_by(pet.Group) |>
  mutate(group_pp = sum(total_losses) / sum(policy.Exposure)) |> #using expos wtd PP
  group_by(pet.Group, pet.Breed) |>
  summarize(
    n_policies = n(),
    breed_pp = sum(total_losses) / sum(policy.Exposure),
    group_pp = first(group_pp),
    diff = breed_pp - group_pp,
    pct_diff = (breed_pp - group_pp) / group_pp,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Focus on top positive and negative outliers
  arrange(desc(abs(pct_diff))) |>
  slice_head(n = 24) |>
  mutate(
    type = ifelse(diff > 0, "Adverse (+ Surcharge)", "Favorable (- Discount)"),
    breed_label = paste0(pet.Breed, " (", pet.Group, ")"),
    breed_label = reorder(breed_label, diff),
    label_text = paste0(ifelse(pct_diff > 0, "+", ""), round(pct_diff * 100), "%")
  )

ggplot(breed_outliers, aes(y = breed_label)) +
  # Connecting line showing the gap/deviation
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = group_pp, xend = breed_pp, yend = breed_label),
    color = "grey65", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  # Group Benchmark Point
  geom_point(aes(x = group_pp, fill = "Group Benchmark"), size = 3.5, shape = 21, stroke = 1) +
  # Breed Observed Point (colored by direction)
  geom_point(aes(x = breed_pp, fill = type), size = 3.8, shape = 21, stroke = 1) +
  # Percentage Deviation Label
  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = pmax(group_pp, breed_pp) + 25,
      label = label_text,
      color = type
    ),
    size = 3.5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0
  ) +
  # Color styling
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Premium Level",
    values = c(
      "Group Benchmark"        = "#5B9BD5",  # Blue
      "Adverse (+ Surcharge)"  = "#C00000",  # Red
      "Favorable (- Discount)" = "#385723"   # Green
    )
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Adverse (+ Surcharge)"  = "#C00000",
      "Favorable (- Discount)" = "#385723"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::dollar_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15)) # room for % labels
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Top Outlier Breeds vs. Parent Group Benchmark Pure Premium",
    subtitle = "Blue = Expected Group PP | Colored = Actual Breed PP (with % deviation)",
    x = "Pure Premium ($)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linetype = "dotted", color = "grey80"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 10),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9.5)
  )
```

## 9.3 Interaction Effects

pet.Age shows the highest correlation with pure premium, and is the only variable that our competitor insurance carrier,
uses. However, in veterinary science, an 8-year-old animal doesn't have the same risk profile across species or sizes. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23535614/)

```{r}
analyze_int_age_by_var <- function(df, col){
  col_name <- rlang::as_name(ensym(col))
  age_by_col <- df |> 
    mutate(age_band = cut(pet.Age, breaks = c(0,5,9,13,17,30),
            labels=c("0-5","5-9","9-13","13-17","17+")))  |> 
    group_by(age_band, {{col}}) |> 
    summarize(mean_pp = round(mean(pure_premium),2),
              .groups = "drop") |> 
    mutate({{col}} := forcats::fct_reorder(as.factor({{col}}), mean_pp, .fun = max, .desc = TRUE)) 
  
  age_by_col |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from = {{col}}, values_from = mean_pp)
  
  age_by_col |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = age_band, y = mean_pp, color = {{col}}, group = {{col}}), linetype = Species) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
    labs(
      title = glue("Mean Pure Premium by pet.Age band and {col_name}"),
      x = "Age Band",
      y = "Mean Pure Premium ($)",
      color = col_name,
    )
}
  
```

### With pet.Age

#### pet.Gender

```{r}
analyze_int_age_by_var(df, pet.Gender)
```

No significant interaction here.

```{r}
analyze_int_age_by_var(df, pet.Offspring)
```

No significant interaction here.

#### pet.Type

```{r}
analyze_int_age_by_var(df, pet.Type)
```

pet.Type shows significant interaction with age, owning to the differences in slope for the last
two age bands.

Let's see if pet.Group provides any improvement over it.

#### pet.Group

```{r}
train |>
  mutate(age_band = cut(pet.Age, breaks = c(0, 5, 9, 13, 17, 30),
                        labels = c("0-5", "5-9", "9-13", "13-17", "17+"))) |>
  group_by(age_band, pet.Group) |>
  summarize(
    mean_pp = round(mean(pure_premium), 2),
    # Extract species (each group/breed is exclusively Cat or Dog)
    Species = first(pet.Type),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Order legend by peak height
  mutate(pet.Group := forcats::fct_reorder(as.factor(pet.Group), mean_pp, .fun = max, .desc = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(
    x        = age_band,
    y        = mean_pp,
    color    = pet.Group,
    group    = pet.Group,
    linetype = Species
  )) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    # Set Dog = dotted, Cat = solid
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Dog" = "dotted", "Cat" = "solid")) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
    labs(
      title    = glue("Mean Pure Premium by pet.Age band and pet.Group"),
      x        = "Age Band",
      y        = "Mean Pure Premium ($)",
      color    = glue("Pet Group (by peak)"),
      linetype = "Species"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

Clearly, pet.Type is a more solid candidate with Age interaction as it captures that
change in slope with age which all the pet.Group candidates mimic.

We can keep pet.Type as an interaction with age, and pet.Group as an independent
categorical variable which also captures the signal from pet.Type.

#### pet.Microchip
